## Why This Matters

Two debts from earlier lessons come due today. In L02 you swept k = 1, 15, 51 and
were told that choosing such knobs "gets a principled treatment in Unit III". In
L08 you watched gamma=100 score 0.996 on training and 0.840 on test, and we named
it *overfitting* — but we caught it by peeking at the test set, which (you are
about to learn) is itself a methodological sin.

This lesson pays both debts: **why** flexible models betray you, and **how** to
set their dials without contaminating the one number you must keep honest.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
Studying for an exam from past papers. Memorize the answer key word for word and
you ace every past paper while failing the real exam — **overfitting**. Skim so
casually you learn nothing and you fail both — **underfitting**. And if you "check
your readiness" against the real final, then study some more, repeatedly — your
eventual score proves nothing, because the final leaked into your studying. That
last one is what tuning on the test set does.
:::

## The Flexibility Dial

Every model family you have met carries at least one knob that sets how much the
model can bend:

| Model | Knob | More flexible when... |
|-------|------|----------------------|
| kNN (L02) | k | k is *small* (each prediction trusts one neighborhood) |
| logistic regression (L04) | — (plain form) | a fixed, linear shape — the rigid baseline |
| SVM (L08) | C, gamma, kernel | C large, gamma large, kernel nonlinear |

These knobs are **hyperparameters**: settings *you* choose before fitting, as
opposed to parameters (coefficients, support vectors) the algorithm learns from
data. L02 used the word in passing; this lesson is its formal home. The question
of the day: **where do you set the dial?**

## Underfitting and Overfitting

Turn any flexibility dial across its range and score the model twice — on the data
it trained on, and on data it has never fit — and a universal pattern appears:

| Position | Training score | Validation score | Diagnosis |
|----------|---------------|------------------|-----------|
| too flexible | excellent (even perfect) | clearly worse | **overfitting** — the model memorized noise |
| sweet spot | good | nearly as good | what you want |
| too rigid | mediocre | mediocre (converged with training) | **underfitting** — the model cannot express the pattern |

The distance between the two scores is the **generalization gap**. Reread L08's
gamma experiment as a worked diagnosis: gamma=100 gave train 0.996 / test 0.840 —
a 0.156 gap, overfit; gamma=1 gave 0.960 / 0.893 — a healthy 0.067. The lab draws
this table as a curve, with k as the dial.

## Bias and Variance: Why the Dial Behaves This Way

Two distinct sources of error sit behind that table.

- **Bias** is systematic error from rigidity: the model family *cannot* represent
  the true pattern, so it misses in the same direction no matter which training
  sample you give it. A straight line through a curved boundary has high bias.
- **Variance** is sensitivity to the draw: give the model a *different* random
  training sample and it produces a noticeably different boundary. A k=1
  classifier — whose boundary threads around every single training point — has
  high variance: new sample, new thread.

::: {.callout-note title="The dartboard picture"}
Imagine refitting the same model family on many alternative training sets and
plotting each fit's predictions as one dart. **High bias** = the darts cluster
tightly in the *wrong* place (consistent, consistently off). **High variance** =
the darts scatter widely around the right place (sometimes great, never
dependable). Low bias *and* low variance — a tight cluster on the bullseye — is
the goal, and for a fixed dataset the flexibility dial moves you along a trade:
rigidity buys consistency at the cost of expressiveness; flexibility buys
expressiveness at the cost of stability.
:::

That trade is the **bias-variance dilemma**: turning the dial toward flexibility
lowers bias and raises variance; turning it back does the reverse. Total error
carries both (plus noise nothing can remove — the formula is in the Deep Dive),
so the best dial setting is wherever their *sum* bottoms out.

## The U-Curve

Plot validation error against flexibility and the dilemma becomes one picture: a
**U**. The left wall (too rigid) is bias; the right wall (too flexible) is
variance; the bottom of the U is the sweet spot. Training error, plotted
alongside, climbs steadily toward the flexible end — small wiggles aside, it peaks
at the most flexible setting — which is precisely why it cannot be used to choose:
it always ends up voting for the most flexible model on offer.

Honesty note: on easy or noisy data the U can be lopsided — the lab's coqui curve
has a sharp overfitting cliff on the flexible side but only a shallow underfitting
plateau on the rigid side. Diagnose from the *pattern of the two curves*, not from
expecting a picture-perfect U.

## Why You Cannot Tune on the Test Set

The test set exists to answer exactly one question — *how will this model do on
data nobody has seen?* — and it can only answer it **once**. The moment a
hyperparameter is chosen *because* it scored best on the test set, the test set
has participated in building the model: of all the candidates, you kept the one
that best flattered those particular examples, part skill and part luck. The
resulting score is inflated, and no honest number remains.

::: {.callout-important}
Treat the test set as a **sealed envelope**. Every decision — which model family,
which hyperparameters, which features — must be made without it. It is opened
once, at the end, and its verdict is final. Repeated "just checking" is the same
leak in slow motion.
:::

So model selection needs held-out data that is *not* the test set — data the
model didn't fit, drawn from inside the training set.

## Validation Sets and k-Fold Cross-Validation

The simple version: carve a **validation set** out of the training data (a
three-way split: train / validation / test), fit candidates on the reduced
training portion, compare them on the validation slice, keep the test envelope
sealed. Its weakness on small datasets: which calls land in that one slice is a
lottery — the lab measures a 0.178 accuracy spread across slices for the *same
model*.

**k-fold cross-validation** fixes the lottery by rotation: split the training
data into k equal folds (5 is the workhorse), then run k rehearsals — each fold
takes one turn as validator while the others train — and average the k scores:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  D["Training data<br/>(the test set is NOT here)"] --> F["Split into 5 folds"]
  F --> R1["Rehearsal 1:<br/>validate on fold 1,<br/>train on folds 2-5"]
  F --> R2["Rehearsal 2:<br/>validate on fold 2,<br/>train on folds 1, 3-5"]
  F --> R3["... rehearsals 3-5,<br/>each fold validates once"]
  R1 --> A["Average the 5 scores:<br/>the CV accuracy"]
  R2 --> A
  R3 --> A
```

Every training example gets to be validation data exactly once, no example ever
validates a model it helped fit, and the average is far steadier than any single
rehearsal. In scikit-learn this whole diagram is one call:
`cross_val_score(model, X_train, y_train, cv=5)`.

## The Model Selection Protocol

The recipe the lab drills, worth memorizing as a unit:

1. **Grid:** list candidate dial settings (k in {1, 3, 5, ...}).
2. **Cross-validate** each candidate on the training data only.
3. **Pick** the setting with the best mean CV score.
4. **Refit** the winner on *all* the training data (the folds were rehearsals;
   the performance uses every training example).
5. **Open the envelope:** score the refit model on the test set, once. Report
   that number.

## When to Use / When NOT to Use

- **Use CV when:** datasets are small-to-medium (where one validation split is a
  lottery); whenever you compare hyperparameters or model families; whenever a
  result is headed into a report.
- **Think twice when:** training is very expensive (k folds = k retrainings —
  deep networks in Unit V often fall back to a single validation split, made
  viable by their huge datasets); data has time order (random folds leak the
  future into the past — time-series splitting exists, out of scope here).

## Common Pitfalls

- **Tuning on the test set** — the headline sin; the lab runs the trap once,
  labeled, so you recognize it (it "improved" 0.840 to 0.867, fictitiously).
- **Peeking repeatedly.** Checking the test set after every tweak is tuning on it
  in slow motion. One look, at the end.
- **Panicking over CV-vs-test disagreement.** CV said 0.849, test said 0.840 —
  both are estimates with sampling noise (look at the fold spread). Small gaps
  are expected; investigate only when the gap is large.
- **Forgetting the refit.** The CV winner was judged while trained on 4/5 of the
  data; ship the version refit on all of it (protocol step 4).

::: {.callout-note title="Deep Dive: the decomposition behind the dilemma (Optional)" collapse="true"}

For squared-error prediction, the expected error of a model family at a point
decomposes exactly:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[(y - \hat{f}(x))^2\big] = \underbrace{\text{Bias}\big[\hat{f}(x)\big]^2}_{\text{systematic miss}} + \underbrace{\text{Var}\big[\hat{f}(x)\big]}_{\text{sample-to-sample wobble}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{irreducible noise}}$$

The expectation runs over alternative training samples — the "many darts" of the
dartboard picture. Bias is how far the *average* dart lands from the truth;
variance is how scattered the darts are around their own average; $\sigma^2$ is
the noise floor no model can beat (the coqui species genuinely overlap, so even
the perfect classifier errs there). Flexibility moves error between the first two
terms; nothing moves the third. The derivation is three lines of algebra from
adding and subtracting $\mathbb{E}[\hat{f}(x)]$ — ISL ch. 2 walks it.
:::

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Why not just use the most flexible model and lots of data?"** — More data
genuinely is the antidote to variance: with enough examples, flexible models stop
wobbling, which is the bet deep learning makes (Unit V). But data is never
infinite, labeling is expensive, and for the dataset you actually have, the
dilemma stands — which is why this lesson's machinery stays mandatory even in the
deep-learning era.

**"CV said 0.849 but the test said 0.840 — is cross-validation broken?"** — No;
it would be suspicious if they matched exactly. Both numbers estimate the same
unknown quantity from finite samples; the lab's fold scores ranged 0.733 to 0.911
around their 0.849 mean. Read CV scores with error bars in mind, and treat
small CV-vs-test gaps as the sampling noise they are.

**"How many folds should I use?"** — 5 or 10 is the industry default and fine for
this course. More folds means more retraining and smaller validation slices; the
extreme — one fold per example — is leave-one-out CV, occasionally useful on tiny
datasets, expensive everywhere else. (And when the grid of hyperparameters gets
big, `GridSearchCV` automates the loop you wrote by hand in the lab — same
protocol, less typing.)

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---------|---------------|
| Hyperparameter | a dial you set before fitting (k, C, gamma) — not learned |
| Overfitting | memorized the sample: big train-vs-validation gap |
| Underfitting | too rigid for the pattern: both scores mediocre and converged |
| Bias | systematic miss from rigidity |
| Variance | boundary wobbles with the training draw |
| The dilemma | flexibility lowers bias, raises variance; minimize the sum |
| Test set | a sealed envelope, opened once, never used for choosing |
| k-fold CV | k rehearsals, every fold validates once, average the scores |
| Protocol | grid, CV, pick, refit on all training data, test once |
